newsitem.title: USA: Congressman cites "evidence" of tobacco conspiracy.
newsitem.headline: Congressman cites "evidence" of tobacco conspiracy.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, U.S. Law Correspondent
The congressman who sought the current criminal probe of the tobacco industry said he had a "smoking gun" document showing manufacturers and their lawyers conspired to hide the dangers of cigarettes.
Rep. Martin Meehan, a Massachusetts Democrat, said on Monday he had obtained a confidential 1964 report, which appears to have been written for Britain's Tobacco Research Council.

The document is based on meetings that two researchers had in the United States from Sept. 10, 1964, through Oct. 15, 1964, with the presidents, officers and lawyers for major U.S. and British tobacco companies at which they discussed how they were handling health research and trial strategy.

The document says that at the time, some tobacco executives firmly believed there was no proof that smoking was harmful to health, while others, including the president of the tobacco unit of Philip Morris Cos. Inc., "hedge a little."
In fact, the document says, the then president had "stopped assuring his stockholders annually that he is confident that smoking will eventually be exonerated."
Another part of the document discusses the executives' views on the importance of nicotine.
One person quoted is William Blunt, then president of Liggett & Meyers, which is now Liggett Group Inc. and owned by Loews Corp.
"Mr. Blunt firmly held the view that people smoked because of the nicotine," the report says.
A Liggett spokesman had no comment.
The tobacco industry denies that nicotine is addictive, and the heads of the major companies testified to this in 1994 congressional hearings.

The document also describes the power U.S. lawyers had over manufacturers' health research activity and the information released because of the fear of costly litigation. It describes a "policy committee" made up of lawyers from the major tobacco companies that reported directly to the presidents.
"I think this document is a smoking gun. It is the best evidence of collusion, of a conspiracy on the part of all the companies and their lawyers," Meehan told Reuters.
Meehan said the document had been sent to him anonymously.
Lawyers involved in tobacco litigation said the document recently surfaced in a second-hand-smoking lawsuit in Mississippi when the defendants withdrew their claim that it was confidential.
Spokesmen for major tobacco companies said the document was unimportant, had been taken out of context and was merely a "snapshot" of work done by two British researchers about 32 years ago.
Michael York, a Philip Morris spokesman, said Meehan had misconstrued information in the report and had used it to portray an "inaccurate image" of the industry.

"It shows to me the congressman misunderstood something quite common and routine in litigation. ... Companies work very hard to coordinate their legal defense. ... It's inconceiveable to me that lawyers would not play such an important part in an industry facing so many legal and regulatory challenges."

Meehan said he planned to turn the document over to the Justice Department, which is currently investigating whether the major tobacco companies withheld information from federal agencies about the health risks of smoking.

Meehan said he planned to suggest that the document supported a 1994 memo he sent to the Justice Department outlining possible areas of alleged criminal activity, including the role of lawyers in alleged coverups.
Plaintiffs' lawyers said the document could also be used in the growing litigation against the tobacco industry by states and individuals.
One section of the document is devoted to the lawyers' policy committee and its concerns about litigation.
"In consequence of the importance of the lawsuits, the main power in the smoking and health situation undoubtedly rests with the lawyers," the report says.
It says the committee's policy, "very understandably, in effect is 'don't take any chances.'"

"It is a situation that does not encourage constructive or bold approaches to smoking and health problems and it also means that the Policy Committee of lawyers exercises close control over all aspects of the problems," the document says.
